name: From Wax Cylinder to Earbud: Recorded Sound
description: Edison's phonograph, the radio, vinyl, cassettes, the Walkman, CDs, MP3s and streaming: how people learned to capture music and voices and carry them around.

checkpoints.name: Wax and wireless
checkpoints.note: Thomas Edison's phonograph cylinder first played back a voice. Guglielmo Marconi and others made radio work, and by 1922 the BBC was broadcasting to listeners at home.

checkpoints.name: Voices from the screen and air
checkpoints.note: Sound film arrived, and The Jazz Singer in 1927 made it a hit. Radio drama such as The War of the Worlds in 1938 showed how a broadcast could grip a nation.

checkpoints.name: Vinyl, tape and transistors
checkpoints.note: The LP record held a long stretch of music on one side. The transistor radio made listening portable, and the compact cassette and 8-track tape put music in cars and pockets.

checkpoints.name: The disc and the pocket
checkpoints.note: Sony's Walkman made private listening normal, and the compact disc moved music to digital form. The CD Walkman, Sound Blaster, MiniDisc, MP3 and Winamp followed as computers became players.

checkpoints.name: Streams and downloads
checkpoints.note: Napster showed the appetite for online music, and the iPod and the iTunes Store sold songs by download. SoundCloud, Bandcamp, Spotify and Apple Music later turned music into a stream.
